Supply only the token value. Including the word `Bearer` in the value would
produce a second prefix in the outgoing header. Static Bearer mode has no
refresh behavior; an expired token must be replaced outside apibackuper.
Template: `examples/templates/bearer-auth.yaml`.

## API keys

```yaml
auth:
  type: apikey
  api_key: "${CATALOG_API_KEY}"
  api_key_header: X-API-Key
```

Change `api_key_header` only if the service requires a different header name,
for example `X-Catalog-Key`. There is no `api_key_file` setting; use an environment
variable for this method. For another custom authentication header, a trusted
hook can supply it, subject to the project's normal auth-header precedence.

## OAuth2 refresh

Obtain an access token outside apibackuper, then configure:

```yaml
auth:
  type: oauth2
  token: "${ACCESS_TOKEN}"
  auth_url: https://api.example.com/oauth/token
  refresh_token: "${REFRESH_TOKEN}"
```

`token_file` can replace the inline access token. The refresh token is supplied
through `refresh_token`, including environment expansion; there is no separate
refresh-token-file option.

The refresh sequence is:

1. Send the API request with the current Bearer token.
2. If it returns HTTP 401, POST form fields `grant_type=refresh_token` and
   `refresh_token` to `auth_url`.
3. Require HTTP 200 with JSON containing `access_token`, for example:

```json
{"access_token": "replacement-access-token", "refresh_token": "replacement-refresh-token"}
```

4. Keep the new access token and optional rotated refresh token in memory, then
   retry the original API request with its original body/query and new header.

Refresh uses configured connection/read timeouts and SSL verification. It is
triggered by a 401, and also before a request when the last token response gave
an `expires_in` that ends within 60 seconds; a 403 does not trigger it. Without
an initial `token`, the first token is requested before the first API request.
When `client_id` is set, the refresh request authenticates the client as
described below. Refresh failures are logged and the unsuccessful request is
handled by the normal [HTTP error policy](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/rate-limiting-and-requests).

## OAuth2 client credentials

For machine-to-machine APIs, let apibackuper request tokens itself:

```yaml
auth:
  type: oauth2
  grant_type: client_credentials
  auth_url: https://auth.example.com/oauth/token
  client_id: backup-client
  client_secret: "${OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}"
  scope: "catalog.read"
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|-------|---------|---------|
| `grant_type` | `refresh_token` | `client_credentials` requests tokens with the client's own credentials |
| `client_id` | none | Client identifier |
| `client_secret` / `client_secret_file` | none | Client secret, inline (prefer `${VAR}`) or read from a file |
| `scope`, `audience` | omitted | Sent with the token request when set |
| `client_auth_method` | `client_secret_basic` | `client_secret_basic` sends HTTP Basic; `client_secret_post` sends `client_id` and `client_secret` in the form body |

Before the first API request, apibackuper POSTs `grant_type=client_credentials`
(plus `scope` and `audience`) to `auth_url` and sends the returned
`access_token` as a Bearer header. It requests a new token when the current one
is within 60 seconds of its `expires_in`, and after a 401, then retries the
rejected request once. Parallel page requests share one token request.

A failed token request stops the run before any API request is sent without
credentials. A missing or empty `client_secret_file` is a configuration error.
Logs and error messages never include the client secret or tokens.

### Restart and provider limitations

Refreshed tokens are **not persisted** to YAML, the environment or `token_file`.
If the provider invalidates an old refresh token on rotation, arrange to provision
current credentials before restarting or resuming. Reusing the original file
cannot recover a rotated refresh token automatically.

Browser authorization and authorization-code/PKCE grants are not implemented.
Providers that require them need external token management.

## Header precedence and scope

`headers.json` can add ordinary headers such as `Accept` or a client identifier.
The auth handler overrides a conflicting authentication header when constructing
the request. Use one source for a given credential instead of maintaining both
`Authorization` in JSON and `auth` in YAML.

Follow and attachment requests also receive the project's authentication.
Use URLs that are allowed to receive those credentials, especially when records
contain absolute URLs on another host. When a response redirects to another
host, `Authorization`, the configured API-key header and other headers with
credential-like names (`Cookie`, `X-Auth-Token`, `api_key`, …) are dropped from
the redirected request. The optional aria2 downloader is a
separate service and does not inherit the built-in authentication policy.

## Check authentication problems

| Symptom | What to verify |
|---------|----------------|
| Unresolved variable error | Variable is exported in the shell/service launching the command; `.env` is not automatic |
| No usable token from a file | Absolute path, readability, non-empty content and absence of an overriding inline value |
| HTTP 401 | Token value/prefix, expiry, endpoint, account and supported refresh configuration |
| HTTP 403 | Token permissions and API access policy; OAuth refresh is only triggered by 401 |
| Restart breaks OAuth refresh | Provider rotates refresh tokens; the previous process did not persist the new value |
| Dry-run succeeds but API rejects credentials | Dry-run checks local configuration and reports auth type; it makes no authentication request |

Use `--verbose` on commands that support it and inspect the log. Recognized
credential fields are redacted in shared diagnostics, but custom hook output
and API-specific free text still need care before sharing. See
[protected APIs](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/use-cases/protected-apis) for a complete operational example.

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/rate-limiting-and-requests

# Rate limiting and requests

These settings control different parts of a request: `rate_limit` controls when
an attempt may start, `request` controls the exchange and retry budget, and
`error_handling` controls what the page collector does after a request fails.
Configure them together for a predictable long-running backup.

## A conservative starting policy

```yaml
project:
  default_delay: 0
rate_limit:
  enabled: true
  requests_per_second: 2
  requests_per_minute: 100
  burst_size: 1
request:
  connect_timeout: 10
  read_timeout: 60
  verify_ssl: true
  parallelism: 1
  retry:
    max_retries: 3
    backoff_strategy: exponential
    initial_delay: 1
    max_delay: 10
    retry_on_status: [429, 500, 502, 503, 504]
error_handling:
  max_consecutive_errors: 3
  continue_on_error: false
```

Merge these sections into a complete project. This example allows a small
request rate, retries transient responses, and stops collection after a page
cannot be fetched. Increase concurrency only after confirming the API's quota
and stable pagination behavior.

## Rate limits and bursts

| Field | Effective default | Behavior |
|-------|-------------------|----------|
| `enabled` | true when the section exists | false disables this project's limiter |
| `requests_per_second` | No per-second cap | Positive number; token refill rate, fractions allowed |
| `requests_per_minute` | No minute cap | Integer rolling 60-second window; 0 disables this window |
| `requests_per_hour` | No hour cap | Integer rolling 3,600-second window; 0 disables this window |
| `burst_size` | 5 | Positive token-bucket capacity and initial allowance |

Without a `rate_limit` section there is no configured limiter. Merely adding
`enabled: true` without any quota does not create a rate cap. Omit a per-second
limit to disable it; validation rejects an explicitly non-positive value.

All configured windows apply. For example, 10 requests/second with a limit of
100/minute can still stop for the minute window after 100 requests. A token
bucket with `burst_size: 5` can start with five tokens; it does not enforce evenly
spaced requests. Use `burst_size: 1` when a service tolerates little burst traffic.

Limits are shared by the project's ordinary request attempts in this process,
including retries. They are not coordinated across separate CLI processes or
other applications using the same account. Redirects, OAuth token refresh and
its immediate replay can add HTTP exchanges inside an attempt; reserve quota
headroom when the provider counts every exchange. aria2 transfers use their own
service policy.

## Concurrency and default delay

`request.parallelism` defaults to 1 and controls concurrent **backup page**
requests. It is not a global worker count for follow or file downloads. Pages
are consumed in order for durable checkpoints; extra requests can already be
in flight when an end page or failure is discovered.

`project.default_delay` defaults to 0.5 seconds and sleeps after a successful
request. It adds to response time and any rate-limit waits. With multiple
workers, each successful request waits independently, so this setting alone
does not impose an account-wide requests/second cap. Use `rate_limit` for quotas.

## Connection and read timeouts

```yaml
request:
  connect_timeout: 10
  read_timeout: 60
```

`connect_timeout` defaults to 30 seconds; `read_timeout` defaults to 120 seconds.
Both are positive integer seconds. The first bounds connection establishment;
the second bounds waiting for data during reads, not total job duration. A slow
stream can take longer than `read_timeout` overall while continuing to deliver data.

The legacy `request.timeout` defaults to 120 but does not replace the active
connection/read pair. Set those fields explicitly. Total wall time also includes
retries, backoff, rate-limit waits, redirects and successful-request delays.

## Retry budget and delay calculation

```yaml
request:
  retry:
    max_retries: 3
    backoff_strategy: exponential
    initial_delay: 1
    max_delay: 4
    retry_on_status: [429, 500, 502, 503, 504]
```

`max_retries` counts retries **after** the initial attempt: 3 permits up to four
ordinary attempts. Retryable transport failures and configured unsuccessful
statuses consume this budget. Other unsuccessful statuses fail without exhausting
it, after any supported OAuth refresh attempt. HTTP 2xx is considered successful;
an application error encoded inside a 200 JSON body requires correct extraction
or application-specific handling.

For this example, delays before retries are 1, 2 and 4 seconds. `fixed` uses
`initial_delay` each time, capped by `max_delay`; exponential uses
`min(initial_delay * 2^(retry_number - 1), max_delay)`.
A server `Retry-After: 15` overrides the configured backoff delay, even when it
exceeds `max_delay`. An HTTP-date Retry-After waits until that time; otherwise the configured
delay is used instead.

`retry.wait_headers` lists the headers read, in order, for that server wait
(default `["Retry-After"]`). Values can be seconds, an HTTP date, or a Unix
timestamp such as GitHub's `X-RateLimit-Reset`; numbers of at least 10^9 are read
as Unix time. `retry.max_wait` fails the request instead of sleeping longer:

```yaml
request:
  retry:
    max_retries: 5
    wait_headers: [Retry-After, X-RateLimit-Reset, RateLimit-Reset]
    max_wait: 900
```

POST requests can also be retried. Use this tool for read/query endpoints where
replaying a request is acceptable to the API; it does not provide an idempotency-key
or write-transaction protocol.

### Retry configuration precedence

For each corresponding setting, flat compatibility keys override nested keys:

1. Explicit `request.retry_max_retries`, `retry_backoff_strategy`,
   `retry_initial_delay`, `retry_max_delay`, `retry_on_status`.
2. Nested values under `request.retry`.
3. Fallbacks: `project.retry_count` (5), `project.retry_delay` (5 seconds),
   fixed backoff and maximum delay `max(retry_delay, retry_delay * 4)`.

The fallback retry status list is `error_handling.retry_on_errors`, or
`[429, 500, 502, 503, 504]` when omitted. Configure a non-empty explicit list to
remove ambiguity. Prefer the nested YAML form and
remove leftover flat overrides when migrating a configuration.

## Response rules

The HTTP status alone does not always tell whether a response is usable. Some
APIs answer `200` with `{"error": "quota exceeded"}` or an HTML maintenance
page; others answer `404` for an empty result. `request.response_rules` is an
ordered list; the first rule whose conditions all match decides:

```yaml
request:
  response_rules:
    - body_key: error          # a JSON body with an "error" field
      action: retry
    - content_type: text/html  # a maintenance page instead of JSON
      action: fail
    - status: 404
      body_key: items          # 404 with an empty list means "no data"
      action: accept
    - status: [403, 451]
      action: missing
```

| Condition | Matches when |
|-----------|--------------|
| `status` | The status equals the code, is in the list, or is in a class such as `4xx` |
| `body_key` | The dotted path exists in a JSON body; with `body_value`, it also equals that value |
| `content_type` | The `Content-Type` header contains the text (case-insensitive) |

| Action | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `retry` | Retry under the retry policy, even for a 2xx response; fail when the budget runs out |
| `fail` | Fail without retrying |
| `missing` | Follow and `getfiles` record the object as gone and continue; a page request fails |
| `accept` | Treat the response as successful, even with a non-2xx status |

A rule needs at least one condition; `validate-config` checks rule shape. When
no rule matches, the status policy applies as before: 2xx succeeds, configured
statuses are retried, and 404/410 count as missing for follow and file
downloads. The run summary counts how often each action was applied.

## Failed pages and continued collection

```yaml
error_handling:
  retry_on_errors: [429, 500, 502, 503]
  max_consecutive_errors: 10
  continue_on_error: true
```

After a page exhausts its HTTP retry budget, `continue_on_error: true` lets the
collector try later pages until the consecutive-error limit is reached. A
successfully saved page resets the consecutive-error count. `false` stops at
the first unresolved failure; parallel requests may already have completed.

Continued collection is still an **incomplete run**: it returns a nonzero exit,
does not publish a failed full backup or advance successful update state, and
keeps recovery progress. The checkpoint only advances through the contiguous
saved prefix. Use the matching `run full --resume` or `update --resume` to retry
from the first unresolved page.

## SSL and redirects

| Field | Default | Notes |
|-------|---------|-------|
| `verify_ssl` | true | Boolean only; a CA-bundle path is not accepted in this option |
| `allow_redirects` | true | Follow redirects using the HTTP client; credential headers are dropped when the host changes |
| `max_redirects` | 5 | Maximum followed redirects; 0 permits none |
| `user_agent` | `apibackuper/<version>` | Session User-Agent; per-request headers may override it |

Leave SSL verification enabled for normal collection. A self-signed or broken
certificate may require an explicitly trusted test/internal configuration with
`verify_ssl: false`; this logs a warning. Use the final API endpoint rather
than relying on unnecessary redirects, and inspect failures in the log.

## Proxies

Use the currently implemented comma-separated string form, including in YAML:

```yaml
request:
  proxies: "http=http://proxy.example.com:8080,https=http://proxy.example.com:8080"
```

Each entry is `scheme=proxy_url`. An HTTPS target can use an HTTP CONNECT proxy,
so the proxy URL does not need `https://` merely because the target does.
The schema also accepts a YAML mapping, but the current loader does not apply
ordinary mapping entries correctly. Use the string form for an effective
project-level setting. This parser is not a JSON-object-string parser.

The underlying Requests session also uses its normal process environment.
Account for `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` in scheduled environments;
remove unintended inherited proxy settings when diagnosing routing problems.

## Diagnose slow or failing runs

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| Long wait with no requests | Minute/hour quota window, Retry-After and backoff logs |
| Too many requests despite a delay | Multiple workers/processes, token-bucket burst and other account consumers |
| All retries fail on 401/403 | Authentication/permissions; extra retries do not fix an invalid credential |
| Timeout persists after increasing `timeout` | Set active `connect_timeout` and `read_timeout` |
| Proxy configuration has no effect | Use the supported string form and inspect process proxy environment |
| Pages were saved but command failed | An unresolved gap keeps the run incomplete; resume with matching mode/storage |

Feature example: `examples/features/concurrency-retry/`. See
[authentication](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/auth) for OAuth refresh and
[backup completeness](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/getting-started/data-integrity) for consistency limits.

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/project-and-data

# Project and data

These sections answer three questions: which dataset is this, what endpoint
returns it, and which parts of the response are records and metadata? Configure
these before adding follow or file downloads.

## Project identity and recovery files

```yaml
settings:
  name: catalog
  splitter: "."
  logfile: apibackuper.log
  checkpoint_interval_pages: 5
```

| Field | Required / default | Meaning |
|-------|--------------------|---------|
| `name` | Required string | Human-readable project identifier |
| `id` | Optional string | Metadata identifier; does not select the endpoint or storage |
| `initialized` | Optional boolean | Legacy scaffold metadata; setting it true does not fill in other sections |
| `splitter` | `.` | Separator for nested response/record field paths |
| `logfile` | `apibackuper.log` | Log path, relative to the working directory unless absolute |
| `state_file` | Project's `apibackuper_state.json` | Last successful run and update watermark |
| `checkpoint_file` | Project's `apibackuper_checkpoint.json` | Recovery mode, storage path and saved-page progress |
| `checkpoint_interval_pages` | `1` | Non-negative periodic checkpoint interval; 0 disables periodic saves |

Lifecycle checkpoints are written even when the interval is 0. State is
advanced only after a successful backup/update; incomplete collection keeps
the previous successful state. A checkpoint is recovery progress, not a
substitute for the archive or its ZIP journal.

Explicit state/checkpoint paths are used as written. For example,
`state_file: run-state.json` resolves from the process working directory even
when `-p /srv/catalog` points elsewhere. Use absolute overrides for scheduled
jobs, and keep one writer per project. See [recovery](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/run).

## Endpoint and response format

```yaml
project:
  description: Public item catalogue
  url: https://api.example.com/items
  http_mode: GET
  iterate_by: page
  resp_type: json
  default_delay: 0.5
```

| Field | Required / default | How to choose |
|-------|--------------------|---------------|
| `url` | Required HTTP(S) endpoint | Use the list endpoint, with fixed filters in `params.json` |
| `http_mode` | Required `GET` or `POST` | POST sends JSON, not form data |
| `description` | Optional | Explain the source, scope and collection purpose |
| `iterate_by` | `page` | `page`, `skip` or `range`; match the API's pagination contract |
| `resp_type` | `json` | `json`, `xml` or `html`; HTML requires `code.postfetch` |
| `detect` | `false` | Infer selected keys from the initial JSON response; review suggestions first |
| `update_mode` | Conditional | Change-key mode when `data.change_key` exists, otherwise timestamp mode |
| `default_delay` | `0.5` seconds | Pause after a successful request; fractional seconds are supported |
| `retry_count` / `retry_delay` | `5` / `5` seconds | Fallbacks for the active request retry policy |
| `work_modes` | Optional string | Legacy descriptive declaration, not a command allowlist or update filter |
| `force_retry` | Legacy boolean | Use `request.retry` to configure retries |

`detect` cannot infer business semantics such as deletion handling, stable sort
order or the correct update filter. Use `apibackuper detect` to inspect
suggestions and then set explicit fields for repeatable production collection.

## Extract records from a wrapped response

For this response:

```json
{
  "result": {
    "count": 3,
    "pages": 2,
    "items": [
      {"id": 41, "metadata": {"modified": "2026-01-01"}},
      {"id": 42, "metadata": {"modified": "2026-01-02"}}
    ]
  }
}
```

use:

```yaml
data:
  data_key: result.items
  total_number_key: result.count
  pages_number_key: result.pages
  item_key: id
  change_key: metadata.modified
```

`data_key` starts from the response root. `change_key` starts from **each extracted
record**. `total_number_key` and `pages_number_key` start from the response root
and describe counts, not record IDs. If both counts are configured, a usable
record total takes precedence over page count.

`item_key` documents the record identifier in configuration. Current backup and
export paths do not build an index or deduplicate by it. Follow operations need
an explicit `follow.follow_item_key`; a comma-separated `data.item_key` string
does not construct a composite identifier automatically.

### Root arrays and single objects

Omit `data_key` for a root array:

```json
[{"id": 41}, {"id": 42}]
```

The required section can be empty: `data: {}`. A bare object such as `{"id":41}`
is treated as one record. If you configure a `data_key`, it must exist; the
backup fails on a missing configured path instead of treating the response as
an empty dataset. `estimate` still needs `total_number_key` even when a backup
can run without total metadata.

### Field names containing dots

When dots are literal field-name characters, choose a different response-path
separator. For `{"@odata.count":3,"value":[{"id":41}]}`:

```yaml
settings:
  splitter: "/"
data:
  data_key: value
  total_number_key: "@odata.count"
  item_key: id
```

A nested record path would then be `metadata/modified`. This separator also
controls export field lookup. Request-body pagination paths use their own dot
notation; changing `splitter` does not change JSON request construction.

These are object paths, not JSONPath: expressions such as `items[*].id` or
`items[0]` are not supported path syntax.

## XML and HTML responses

XML is parsed into a dictionary using `xmltodict`, then extracted with the same
`data_key` rules. Inspect the parsed shape, especially attributes, namespaces
and elements that appear once versus multiple times. For example, repeated
`<item>` elements under `<response><items>` can be selected by
`response.items.item`. XML text values are strings; a numeric-looking change
key does not automatically become an integer.

HTML needs a trusted extraction script with `process(content)` returning a
JSON-serializable list or wrapped object. Configure `code.postfetch` and a
`data_key` matching that return value. Non-JSON backups save the decoded result
as JSON pages, so exports use the resulting JSON shape. See [hooks and extraction](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/hooks).

## Configure updates

For an API accepting `modified_after`, configure all three parts:

```yaml
project:
  update_mode: by_change_key
params:
  change_key_param: modified_after
data:
  change_key: metadata.modified
```

After a successful run, the largest observed record change key becomes the
next update's filter value. Values must be consistently typed and comparable.
Normalize timestamp strings and timezones; mixed numbers and strings can fail
comparison, and inconsistent date strings need not sort chronologically.

For an API accepting a time boundary independently of record fields:

```yaml
project:
  update_mode: by_timestamp
params:
  update_since_param: updated_since
```

The stored `update_watermark` is the prior successful run's start time in ISO
UTC form; legacy state can fall back to `last_run_end`. The API must accept
that representation and define whether boundary values are included. Without
a saved watermark or the matching request parameter, no update filter is sent.
Run and verify a full backup before relying on selective updates.

`custom_script` is reserved and rejected by update execution. Updates retain
historical generations, including repeated IDs; deletions are not inferred.
See [incremental and update](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/use-cases/incremental-and-update) and
[backup completeness](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/getting-started/data-integrity).

## Diagnose extraction problems

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| Missing `data_key` error | Response wrapper, spelling, separator, and whether the API returned an error object |
| First page only | Pagination parameter configured for the chosen mode; actual returned page size |
| Wrong request estimate | `total_number_key` means records, `pages_number_key` means pages |
| Updates fetch the full dataset | Saved state, `update_mode`, matching request parameter, and API-side filter support |
| Repeated IDs after export | Expected retained history; `item_key` does not deduplicate |

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/hooks

# Hooks

Use lifecycle hooks to customize a backup's page requests or record operational
information. Use extraction scripts when a response body must be transformed
before records can be selected. These extension points have different function
signatures and execution models.

## Choose the extension point

| Need | Configure | Function | Execution |
|------|-----------|----------|-----------|
| Add a header or fixed parameter before a run | `hooks.before_run` | `hook(context)` or `run(context)` | Separate Python process |
| Adjust each page's URL, headers or body parameters | `hooks.before_request` | Same | Separate process per callback |
| Observe a returned page or saved-page progress | `hooks.after_response`, `after_page` | Same | Separate process per callback |
| Observe a successfully published backup | `hooks.after_run` | Same | Separate process |
| Parse HTML or custom non-JSON content | `code.postfetch` | `process(content)` | Main Python process |
| Parse HTML detail responses | `code.follow` | `process(content)` | Main Python process |

Hooks run with the user's filesystem/network permissions. Python's `-I` option
isolates interpreter settings; it does not sandbox a script. Only configure
trusted code. `run full --dry-run` does not execute these scripts.

## Register lifecycle scripts

```yaml
hooks:
  before_run: hooks/before_run.py
  before_request: hooks/before_request.py
  after_response: hooks/after_response.py
  after_page: hooks/after_page.py
  after_run: hooks/after_run.py
```

Each path resolves from the project directory unless absolute. Configure only
the callbacks you need; missing optional entries do nothing. Each configured
file defines `hook(context)` or the fallback name `run(context)`, returns a
JSON-serializable value, and must finish within 30 seconds.

These callbacks belong to `run`/`update`. They are not global middleware for
`estimate`, `detect`, `follow` or `getfiles`.

## Request lifecycle and concurrency

For a normal page-collection run, the sequence is:

```text
before_run
  before_request(page)
  HTTP attempt(s), retries and any OAuth refresh
  after_response(page)
  decode, extract records and save the page
  after_page(page)
  ... remaining pages ...
publish archive and successful state
after_run
```

`before_request` and `after_response` wrap the page fetch, not every transport
attempt inside its retry budget. A failed HTTP fetch has no successful
`after_response` callback. A response can reach `after_response` and still fail
later JSON parsing or record extraction.

With parallel pages, request callbacks can run concurrently and finish out of
order. Saved pages are consumed in order by the collector. Every callback starts
a fresh subprocess: Python globals in a hook file do not persist across calls.
Use concurrency-safe external storage if callbacks need shared state.

## Context and return contract

| Hook | Context keys | Applied return keys |
|------|--------------|---------------------|
| `before_run` | `mode`, `project_path`, `headers`, `params` | `headers`, `params` |
| `before_request` | `mode`, `page`, `url`, `headers`, `params` | `url`, `headers`, `params` |
| `after_response` | Same page request context plus `response` | None |
| `after_page` | `mode`, `page`, `records_processed`, `bytes_written` | None |
| `after_run` | `mode`, `pages_processed`, `records_processed`, `bytes_processed`, `last_page`, `last_change_key`, `errors` | None |

`mode` is `full`, `continue` or `update`. Before-request contexts contain
page-specific parameters after pagination construction. The HTTP executor merges
`auth` headers afterward, so overriding `Authorization` in a hook can still be
superseded by the configured auth handler. Contexts can contain credentials
supplied through JSON files or earlier hooks.

### Modify request headers without losing existing values

Save as `hooks/before_request.py`:

```python
def hook(context):
    headers = dict(context.get("headers", {}))
    headers["X-Archive-Client"] = "nightly"
    return {"headers": headers}
```

The return dictionary overrides named objects; it does not recursively merge
their contents. Returning `{"headers":{"X-Archive-Client":"nightly"}}` alone
would replace the previous header object. Copy existing `params` in the same
way before adding a filter or request field. Return `None` to leave everything
unchanged. Returning a value from the observer hooks does not modify stored data.

`before_run` changes the base parameters, after which pagination/update fields
are applied. `before_request` can alter the page request that is about to be
sent. A hook cannot bypass later URL/body serialization merely by returning an
arbitrary Requests keyword; only the keys in the table are applied.

### Observe response metadata

The `response` object is a JSON snapshot, not a live Requests response:

```json
{
  "status_code": 200,
  "headers": {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
  "url": "https://api.example.com/items?page=2",
  "text": "{\"items\":[{\"id\":42}]}",
  "text_truncated": false
}
```

Text is limited to 2,000 characters and can be absent. Do not parse this preview
as if it were the complete response body. To transform records, use extraction
scripts instead. Response headers, URLs and previews can contain sensitive data.

### Interpret saved-page counters

An `after_page` context can look like:

```json
{"mode":"full","page":2,"records_processed":200,"bytes_written":17640}
```

`records_processed` is **cumulative stored-record progress** for the current
collection, initialized from recovery progress when resuming. `bytes_written`
is the serialized size of this one page, not total bytes. A hook observing a
saved page does not mean the full backup has been published. Recovery checkpoints
only advance through the durable contiguous prefix; telemetry is not a transaction
commit signal for the whole dataset.

`after_run` reports final successful-run counters and an empty `errors` object
on that success path. It is not a failure/finally callback and is not guaranteed
to run during publication-only recovery.

## Failures, stdout and retries

The subprocess wrapper writes the return value as JSON on stdout. Do not print
other text there; that makes the result invalid JSON. stderr is captured and
included in warnings when a subprocess fails; stderr from a successful hook is
not automatically forwarded as normal run logging.

A script exception, nonzero exit, timeout or invalid JSON output logs a warning
and supplies no override. Hook failure does not by itself abort the backup.
If a transformation must be mandatory for correct extraction, an in-process
`code.postfetch` script can fail the command instead.

Callbacks do not have exactly-once delivery. Resume/replay can invoke them again,
and publication recovery can skip normal collection callbacks. Make external
side effects idempotent and do not use `after_run` as the sole audit of whether
archive publication occurred.

## Extraction scripts for HTML

```yaml
project:
  resp_type: html
code:
  postfetch: /srv/catalog/scripts/pagetodata.py
  follow: /srv/catalog/scripts/listtodata.py
```

Each extraction file exposes `process(content)`. `content` is raw response bytes.
The function returns a JSON-serializable list or wrapper matching the configured
`data.data_key` / `follow_data_key`. For example, a response containing one JSON
object per text line could be converted by:

```python
import json


def process(content):
    return [json.loads(line) for line in content.decode("utf8").splitlines() if line.strip()]
```

Set `data: {}` when returning a root list, or return `{"items":[...]}` and set
`data_key: items`. The parser above is an example for that specific line format;
real HTML needs a parser matching its structure. Unlike observer hooks, extraction
exceptions can fail the command. Extractors run inside the main process without
the hook subprocess's 30-second timeout.

Use absolute extraction script paths when the same project runs from different
working directories: legacy call sites can resolve relative paths differently.
Main JSON/XML backup decoding uses built-in parsers; selecting `code.postfetch`
without the relevant response mode does not make it a universal response filter.

## Debug a script

1. Check the function name and script path before a live run.
2. Exercise `hook(context)` with a small representative dictionary, including
   a page number and any fields your code reads.
3. Verify that the returned value can be serialized as JSON and contains only
   supported override keys.
4. Inspect `apibackuper.log` for subprocess errors or invalid JSON warnings.
5. Test a resumed run if the hook has any durable external side effects.

Examples of all lifecycle script names live in `examples/features/hooks/`.

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/follow

# Follow

Many list endpoints return summaries, with another endpoint for each object's
full record. `follow` reads the completed main backup, builds one target per
identifier and writes the detail responses to ZIP archives. Run the main backup
before collecting details.

## Start with one detail endpoint

For list records such as:

```json
{"id": 42, "title": "Item 42", "detail_url": "https://api.example.com/items/42"}
```

merge this section into the project:

```yaml
follow:
  follow_mode: item
  follow_http_mode: GET
  follow_item_key: id
  follow_pattern: "https://api.example.com/items/{id}"
```

Then run:

```bash
apibackuper run full
apibackuper follow full --dry-run
apibackuper follow full
apibackuper export details.jsonl
```

The example requests `/items/42`, saves its JSON response as `42.json` in
`details.zip`, and exports the detail records when that archive exists. The
ID comes from `follow_item_key`; it is not inferred from `data.item_key`.
Dry-run prints a plan but does not prove each source record contains that field.

## Field reference

| Field | Default / requirement | Meaning |
|-------|-----------------------|---------|
| `follow_mode` | Required for execution | `item`, `prefix` or `url`; `drilldown` is not implemented |
| `follow_http_mode` | `GET` | GET query parameters or POST JSON body |
| `follow_item_key` | Required record path | Scalar identifier used to name/store the response and deduplicate targets |
| `follow_pattern` | Required for `item`/`prefix` | URL format string or literal prefix |
| `follow_param` | Optional | Alias for the ID in formatting, also sent as a request parameter |
| `follow_url_key` | Required for `url` | Record path containing the complete detail URL |
| `follow_data_key` | Omitted | Path to records inside the detail response, used in pagination/export |
| `rules` | Optional YAML list | Independent detail-fetch rules, each based on the original main records |

Record paths use `settings.splitter`. Missing `follow_item_key` fails collection;
use a scalar string or number, not a list/object or a comma-separated composite.
Repeated IDs in main backup history produce one target per key in a rule, not
one detail response per historical version.

A detail request answered with HTTP 404 or 410, or matching a `missing`
[response rule](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/rate-limiting-and-requests#response-rules), does not stop the run. The key,
page and status are written to `details.missing.json` (`details_<name>.missing.json`
for a named rule) beside the archive, a warning is printed, and the remaining keys
are fetched. `follow continue` requests missing keys again. Other failures still
stop the run and keep the partial archive for `follow continue`.

## Choose a URL mode

### Format a URL with record fields: item

`item` formats `follow_pattern` with top-level record fields. With the example
above, `{id}` becomes `42`. If the identifier is a nested field, supply an alias:

```yaml
follow:
  follow_mode: item
  follow_item_key: metadata.id
  follow_param: item_id
  follow_pattern: "https://api.example.com/items/{item_id}"
```

For `{"metadata":{"id":42}}`, this formats `/items/42` and also sends
`item_id=42` as a query parameter (or POST body field). Omit `follow_param` when
you only need existing top-level fields for URL formatting and the API should
not receive an extra identifier parameter. Substitution does not URL-encode
path values; use identifiers suitable for the endpoint's path syntax.

### Append an identifier: prefix

```yaml
follow:
  follow_mode: prefix
  follow_item_key: id
  follow_pattern: "https://api.example.com/items/"
```

This concatenates the prefix and ID to form `/items/42`. Include the slash or
other separator in the prefix; it is not inserted automatically.

### Use a URL from the record: url

```yaml
follow:
  follow_mode: url
  follow_item_key: id
  follow_url_key: detail_url
```

The URL is taken from the record and `follow_pattern` is unused. Supply a usable
absolute URL; relative links are not automatically resolved against the main
endpoint. The project's auth and ordinary headers apply to these requests, so
use URLs allowed to receive that authentication.

## Detail parameters and response wrappers

Additional detail-request values belong in `follow_params.json`, beside the
main configuration:

```json
{"language": "en", "include_history": false}
```

They are separate from the main `params.json`. Each request copies these base
values, then adds the ID parameter and rule pagination values when configured.
All rules share this base file; a rule's `params` object configures pagination,
not arbitrary fixed request values.

If a detail response is `{"record":{"id":42,"title":"Item 42"}}`, set
`follow_data_key: record`. For `{"items":[...]}`, use `items`. Omit the field
for a root object or array. This path is separate from the main `data.data_key`.
Detail payloads need to be JSON for built-in export/pagination. HTML detail
responses can be converted with `code.follow`; selecting XML for the main
backup does not automatically decode XML detail responses.

## Multiple independent rules

```yaml
follow:
  rules:
    - name: profile
      follow_mode: item
      follow_item_key: id
      follow_pattern: "https://api.example.com/items/{id}"
    - name: events
      follow_mode: item
      follow_item_key: id
      follow_pattern: "https://api.example.com/items/{id}/events"
      follow_data_key: events
```

Both rules read the original main backup records. The events rule receives the
same list ID as the profile rule; it does not consume the fetched profile.
Automatic org → department → employee traversal is not implemented.
`follow` can also be a YAML list containing these rule objects directly.

Use simple unique names, such as `profile` or `events`; names are sanitized for
archive filenames. Each named rule produces its own ZIP archive.

## Paginate a detail endpoint

Page-based detail pagination is configured inside a rule:

```yaml
follow:
  rules:
    - name: events
      follow_mode: item
      follow_item_key: id
      follow_pattern: "https://api.example.com/items/{id}/events"
      follow_data_key: events
      iterate_by: page
      params:
        page_number_param: page
        page_size_param: per_page
        page_size_limit: 50
        max_pages: 100
```

For each item ID, pages start at 1. Responses are stored as
`42_page_1.json`, `42_page_2.json`, and so on. A page with fewer than 50 extracted
events ends that item's traversal. This loop does not use main-list total-count
metadata. A missing page-size limit falls back to the main project page size;
`max_pages` defaults to 1,000.

Reaching `max_pages` without a short page raises an error rather than publishing
an assumed complete result. Set a positive limit large enough to include the
terminating short/empty page. Use `iterate_by: page` with a `page_number_param`;
this detail loop does not implement the top-level skip/range calculations.

## Output selection and export

| Source backend | Detail output directory |
|----------------|-------------------------|
| ZIP | Directory containing `storage.zip` |
| Filesystem | The configured main storage directory |
| SQLite | Directory containing the database file |

An unnamed rule writes `details.zip`. Named rules write `details_profile.zip`,
`details_events.zip`, etc. Output remains ZIP regardless of the main backend.

When a `follow` section exists and `details.zip` is present, `export` selects it
instead of the main pages and uses the top-level `follow_data_key`. Named archives
are not automatically combined or selected. For a pipeline requiring the normal
export/getfiles commands, use a project with a single unnamed detail rule and
the corresponding top-level extraction key. For separate named results, read
the archives explicitly through [Python storage access](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/development/python-api#direct-storage-access).

Main backup changes do not automatically refresh an existing details archive.
Rerun follow when you need updated details. A reused details archive can otherwise
make a later export show older detail data despite a newer main backup.

## Continue after interruption

`follow full` stages a replacement in `details.zip.partial` (or the named
archive's `.partial`), then publishes it after success. `follow continue`
reuses that staging archive when it exists, or continues the published archive
otherwise, skipping saved response names. Keep ZIP `.journal` sidecars together
with their archive. Follow continuation uses saved objects rather than the
main backup's page checkpoint; there is no `follow --resume` flag.

Changing URL rules or response keys while continuing can mix incompatible
results. Preserve needed output, then use `follow full` for a fresh detail view.
Follow requests use the common authentication, retries and rate limits, but
`request.parallelism` does not parallelize this loop and `hooks.*` are not
invoked here.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| Missing identifier error | `follow_item_key` against each extracted main record |
| URL formatting error | Placeholder names, top-level record fields, and any `follow_param` alias |
| Extra ID query parameter | `follow_param` also supplies a request/body field |
| Only one response page per ID | Rule-level `iterate_by` and `params.page_number_param` |
| `max_pages` failure | Actual page size, `follow_data_key`, ignored pagination parameters or a genuinely larger result |
| Export ignores named results | Automatic selection only uses unnamed `details.zip` |
| Continued run fetches nothing new | Saved names are skipped; use full to refresh changed objects |
| "followed objects are missing upstream" warning | Keys in `details.missing.json` returned 404/410 or matched a `missing` rule |

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/files

# Files

`getfiles` extracts attachment references from saved records and downloads the
referenced bytes. Configure it after you have verified the list or detail
backup; it is a separate command, not an automatic step in `run`.

## Source selection and requirements

The main backend must be ZIP (`storage.storage_type: zip`). Downloaded-file
output can independently be ZIP or filesystem storage. The source is:

| Project configuration | Where references are read |
|-----------------------|---------------------------|
| No `follow` section | Published `storage.zip`, using `data.data_key` |
| A `follow` section exists | Unnamed `details.zip`, using top-level `follow_data_key` |

Named detail archives are not selected automatically. Complete the corresponding
`run`/`follow` before invoking `getfiles`. A configured follow section with no
unnamed detail archive does not fall back to the list pages. Use a separate
project/configuration without follow when the attachments should come from the
list rather than details.

## Download complete URLs

For a record such as:

```json
{"id": 42, "document_url": "https://files.example.com/reports/42.pdf"}
```

use:

```yaml
files:
  fetch_mode: prefix
  root_url: ""
  keys: document_url
  storage_mode: filepath
  file_storage_type: zip
  use_aria2: false
```

An empty prefix leaves the extracted URL unchanged. `storage_mode: filepath`
uses its URL path for the saved filename, so this file is stored as
`reports/42.pdf` inside `storage/files.zip` after filename sanitization.

```bash
apibackuper run full
apibackuper getfiles
```

When references are in detail objects, insert `apibackuper follow full` before
`getfiles` and configure the matching detail extraction key.

## Build URLs from relative paths

For `{"attachment":"reports/42.pdf"}`:

```yaml
files:
  fetch_mode: prefix
  root_url: https://files.example.com/
  keys: attachment
  storage_mode: filepath
  file_storage_type: filesystem
```

This concatenates the strings into
`https://files.example.com/reports/42.pdf`. The prefix must contain any needed
slash. It is not general URL resolution: `root_url` ending in `/` plus a value
starting in `/` produces a double slash.

## Build URLs from document IDs

For `{"document_id":42}` and an endpoint `/documents/42`:

```yaml
files:
  fetch_mode: pattern
  root_url: "https://files.example.com/documents/{}"
  keys: document_id
  storage_mode: id
  default_ext: pdf
  file_storage_type: filesystem
```

`pattern` substitutes the extracted scalar into `{}` using Python string
formatting. The example downloads `/documents/42` and stores `42.pdf` under
`storage/files/`. Choose a default extension only when the API's content type
is known; it does not convert the bytes to that format.

## Field reference

| Field | Requirement / default | Meaning |
|-------|-----------------------|---------|
| `fetch_mode` | Required `prefix` or `pattern` | URL concatenation or `{}` substitution |
| `root_url` | Required string | Literal prefix, empty prefix for complete URLs, or format pattern |
| `keys` | Required comma-separated string | Record paths containing attachment references |
| `storage_mode` | `filepath` | Use URL path; `id` uses the extracted value instead |
| `default_ext` | Omitted | Extension appended to ID-mode filenames |
| `file_storage_type` | `zip` | `zip` or `filesystem`, independent of main ZIP source |
| `use_aria2` | false | Use a running external aria2 RPC service instead of the built-in downloader |
| `max_file_size` | No limit | Skip files larger than this many bytes |

Use keys without spaces around commas, such as `document_url,attachments.url`.
Record paths use `settings.splitter`. Values should be scalar strings/numbers
or simple lists of references, not arbitrary objects. For example:

```json
{"attachments": [{"url": "https://files.example.com/a.pdf"}, {"url": "https://files.example.com/b.pdf"}]}
```

can be discovered using `keys: attachments.url`. Discovered references are
collected into a set, so an identical URL/ID is downloaded only once per cache.
This is independent of `data.item_key` and record identity.

## Filenames and collisions

`filepath` ignores the hostname and query string when choosing the name. URLs
`https://a.example/report.pdf` and `https://b.example/report.pdf`, or two signed
URLs differing only in their query, can map to the same destination filename.
An already saved filename is skipped; it is not compared with remote content.
A download answered with HTTP 404 or 410, or matching a `missing` response rule,
is recorded in `files_skipped.list` with its status as the reason, and the remaining files are downloaded; the
next `getfiles` run tries it again. Other failures stop the command.
Choose references and storage mode that give unique names for your dataset.

`id` uses the extracted value, optionally followed by `default_ext`. It does not
infer a separate ID from a URL. Filename sanitization prevents unsafe path
segments, but does not provide versioning or a content-addressed archive.
In ordinary CLI use, `filepath` derives the name from the URL rather than
`Content-Disposition`.

## Download inventory and discovery cache

With default storage paths, `getfiles` can create:

```text
storage/
  allfiles.csv         # cached discovered values, one per line
  files.zip            # downloaded objects when output is ZIP
  files/               # downloaded objects when output is filesystem
  files.list           # URLs recorded by the built-in downloader
  files_skipped.list   # skipped files: 404/410, missing rules, max_file_size
  files-manifest-sha256.txt  # SHA-256 of every stored file, checked by verify
```

Only the selected output backend receives the built-in file payloads. Despite
its extension, `allfiles.csv` is a line-oriented reference cache, not a table
with record metadata. Later runs read it instead of rescanning source records.

After a new backup/update/follow adds references, remove **only the discovery
cache** to rescan while retaining existing downloads. For example, in Python:

```python
from pathlib import Path

Path("storage/allfiles.csv").unlink(missing_ok=True)
```

Run `getfiles` again. Existing filenames are still skipped. To refresh changed
bytes at an existing name, preserve the old file/archive and use a deliberate
fresh file-output collection; deleting the discovery cache alone is insufficient.
There is no CLI flag for conditional HTTP revalidation or download versioning.

## HTTP policy and large files

The built-in downloader uses the project's authentication, `headers.json`, SSL
verification, connection/read timeouts, retries and rate limits. `params.json`
is not applied as an attachment request body. Follow/file URLs may point at
another host; use endpoints allowed to receive the project authentication.

The built-in downloader streams each response in 1 MB chunks to a temporary
file in the storage directory, hashing it with SHA-256 as it arrives, and then
moves the file into ZIP or filesystem file storage; memory use does not grow
with the file size. A failed or interrupted download leaves no stored file and
no manifest line, so the next `getfiles` downloads it again; partial bytes are
not resumed.

Set `files.max_file_size` (bytes) to skip larger files. A file whose
`Content-Length` exceeds it is not read at all; a file without a declared size
is stopped when the stream passes the limit. Both are recorded in
`files_skipped.list`, and the remaining files are downloaded.

Every stored file is appended to `files-manifest-sha256.txt` beside file
storage (`<sha256>  <name>` per line). [`verify`](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/verify) checks file
storage against it and reports changed, missing and unlisted files. Files saved
by older versions get their line on the next `getfiles` run.

## aria2 integration

Install `aria2p` (or the `recommended` extra), start an aria2 RPC service and
configure `use_aria2: true`. The integration connects to:

```text
http://localhost:6800
RPC secret: empty
Output directory: <storage directory>/files/
```

The client queues URLs and lets aria2 perform the transfers; command completion
does not certify that the queued downloads have completed. The ordinary ZIP file
backend is not populated with those external transfer results. Installing the
Python package alone does not start aria2. RPC host, port and secret are not
configurable through the current project schema.

Project auth headers, retry limits, SSL settings and rate limits are not passed
to aria2 as a download policy. Configure the service separately and prefer the
built-in downloader when the project depends on those settings.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| Unsupported main storage | `getfiles` requires ZIP main storage even with filesystem file output |
| Missing `details.zip` | A follow section selects unnamed details; named rules are not automatic sources |
| No newly linked files found | Remove the stale discovery cache after finishing the updated source backup |
| URL contains duplicated/missing slash | Prefix concatenation is literal; inspect `root_url` and extracted values |
| A different document is skipped | Filename collision or a saved filename whose remote bytes changed |
| aria2 queues fail or never finish | RPC service, local endpoint, empty secret and independent download credentials/policy |

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/storage

# Storage

Storage keeps API page payloads so they can be resumed and exported later.
Choose it independently of the export format: any supported main backend can
produce JSONL, gzip, zstd or Parquet. Follow details and downloaded attachments
have their own output rules.

## Choose a backend

| Backend | Useful when | Main trade-off |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| `zip` | You want a portable page archive and ZIP-source attachment downloads | Durable writes also use journal sidecars during collection |
| `filesystem` | You want to inspect JSON pages directly with file tools | Many files and directories for large histories |
| `sqlite` | You want page payloads in one database and SQL-level inspection | API objects remain JSON BLOBs, not normalized relational rows |

All three support full backup, resume, update generations and export. `getfiles`
currently requires a ZIP main source. Follow reads all three source backends but
always writes ZIP detail archives.

## ZIP configuration and paths

```yaml
storage:
  storage_type: zip
  storage_path: storage
```

For a project `/srv/catalog`, the published archive is
`/srv/catalog/storage/storage.zip`. `storage_path` is a **directory** for ZIP;
setting it to `backup.zip` would create `backup.zip/storage.zip`, not rename
the archive file.

A completed archive can contain:

```text
storage.zip
  page_1.json
  page_2.json
  runs/<run-id>/page_1.json
  runs/<later-run-id>/page_1.json
```

The full backup uses flat page members. Every update receives a separate run
namespace, so page 1 of an update does not overwrite the original page 1.
The JSON pages retain the configured response shape; use `export` to extract
records from a response wrapper.

## Filesystem configuration

```yaml
storage:
  storage_type: filesystem
  storage_path: pages
```

This publishes `/srv/catalog/pages/` with the same relative page names:

```text
pages/
  page_1.json
  page_2.json
  runs/
    <run-id>/
      page_1.json
```

Use a dedicated directory for this backend: full publication replaces the
configured directory, including any unrelated files you placed inside it.
A full run is staged in the sibling `pages.partial/`. Publication can briefly
use `pages.previous/` to preserve the old directory during replacement. Keep a
leftover publication/recovery directory until the matching resume completes;
do not manually merge its pages into the published directory.

Export destinations must be outside this backend's directory. For example,
`/srv/catalog/items.jsonl` is suitable; `/srv/catalog/pages/items.jsonl` is rejected
to protect backup contents.

## SQLite configuration

```yaml
storage:
  storage_type: sqlite
  storage_path: storage/catalog.sqlite
```

A relative path resolves from the project. SQLite expects a **database file**,
not the ZIP-style directory setting. An existing directory, or a path ending
in the platform's directory separator, resolves to `storage.db` inside it.
Prefer an explicit filename to avoid ambiguity across machines.

Tables `pages` and `objects` store `name`, `content` (BLOB) and `created_at`.
A row represents a page/object payload, not one record from the API. Names such
as `runs/<run-id>/page_1.json` remain logical names in the database. You can
inspect page inventory with:

```sql
SELECT name, length(content) AS bytes, created_at
FROM pages
ORDER BY name;
```

A full run uses `catalog.sqlite.partial` before publication. Exporting to the
source database path or an alias of it is rejected. See [Python storage access](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/development/python-api#direct-storage-access)
for reading decoded page bytes through the backend interface.

## Full backups and recovery files

`run full` stages data beside the destination and replaces the previous complete
backup only after successful collection/publication. An interrupted run retains
staging data, the checkpoint and the prior successful state. Starting another
full run without `--resume` starts a fresh staging run.

For default ZIP storage, relevant files can include:

```text
catalog/
  apibackuper.yaml
  apibackuper_state.json
  apibackuper_checkpoint.json
  storage/
    storage.zip                  # previous complete backup
    storage.zip.runs/<id>.zip    # one archive per update generation
    storage.zip.partial          # in-progress replacement
    storage.zip.partial.journal/ # durable pages not yet compacted
```

Each `update` writes its generation (`runs/<id>/page_N.json` and its manifest
and exchange records) to its own `storage.zip.runs/<id>.zip`, so an update
compacts only that small archive instead of rewriting `storage.zip`. Commands
read all archives as one backup; generations stored inside `storage.zip` by
earlier versions stay readable. A new full backup retires the previous
generation archives after publication. Tools that open `storage.zip` directly
do not see newer update generations; use `export` or the storage API.

Inside a published archive, each generation (the root for full backups,
`runs/<id>/` for updates) holds its pages plus `manifest-sha256.txt` and
`run.json`, which [`verify`](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/verify) uses to check the stored bytes.

The ZIP journal saves member data durably before checkpoint progress advances.
It is compacted into the archive on close. A journal next to `storage.zip`
rather than `.partial` can also exist for continued collection or updates.

Keep the correct archive/staging path and its `.journal` together with state and
checkpoint. Do not treat a copied ZIP without its active journal as a complete
copy of an interrupted run. Resume can also complete an interrupted publication
from saved data without downloading again:

```bash
apibackuper run full --resume -p /srv/catalog
apibackuper update --resume -p /srv/catalog
```

Choose the command matching the interrupted operation; the examples are
alternatives. See [run](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/run) for checkpoint compatibility and
[update](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/update) for retained generation recovery.

## Response capture

By default every saved page gets a provenance record in the same generation:

| Member | Content |
|--------|---------|
| `exchange_N.json` | Request method, URL, headers and body; response status, reason, final URL, headers, content type, SHA-256 and length; fetch time (UTC), elapsed time, apibackuper version and run ID |
| `raw_N.<ext>` | The response body exactly as received, when the saved page differs from it (XML or HTML responses) |

Credentials are redacted in exchange records: `Authorization`, API-key and other
credential-like headers, sensitive query and body values, and `Set-Cookie`. The
record's `redacted` field is `true` when anything was replaced.

```yaml
storage:
  storage_type: zip
  capture:
    metadata: true    # write exchange_N.json (default)
    raw_body: auto    # auto (non-JSON responses), always, or never
```

Neither member starts with `page_`, so export, follow, resume and record counts
ignore them; the fixity manifest lists them with the pages, and
`export --format warc` builds WARC records from them. With `metadata: false`,
only pages are written (plus `raw_N` when `raw_body` asks for it).

## Compression and reserved settings

| Field | Accepted value | Current CLI behavior |
|-------|----------------|----------------------|
| `storage_type` | Required `zip`, `filesystem` or `sqlite` | Selects main backend |
| `storage_path` | String; default `storage` | Resolved as above, relative to project unless absolute |
| `compression` | Boolean | Schema-accepted; ZIP CLI storage always uses Deflate |
| `compression_level` | Integer 0–9 | Reserved; does not change CLI compression level |
| `max_file_size` | Non-negative integer bytes | Reserved; no automatic archive splitting |
| `split_files` | Boolean | Reserved; no automatic archive splitting |

Compression of exported `.gz` or `.zst` files is a separate operation. Choosing
a compressed export does not change how backup pages are stored.

## Changing backends or moving a project

Changing `storage_type` or `storage_path` selects a different destination; it
does not convert or move previous data. For a backend change, create a separate
project/destination, perform a fresh full backup and verify an export before
retiring the old archive. There is no built-in ZIP-to-SQLite migration command.

For a completed project move, keep config, scripts and successful state together,
and update absolute paths. For an interrupted run, checkpoint storage references
must still match the configured destination; moving the directory alone may
require restoring its original paths to resume. Explicit relative state,
credential and log overrides still resolve from the working directory.

## Retention and export history

Updates retain historical generations; export emits records from all of them,
including repeated IDs. There is no automatic pruning, deduplication or
restore-to-API command. A fresh successful full run replaces the published main
history, so preserve a verified older archive separately when retention requires it.

Stop writers before copying or rotating an archive. Do not use the same storage
path for simultaneous projects, and do not share checkpoints between them.
If a details archive exists, export may select that archive instead of main
pages; refresh follow results after a changed main backup when appropriate.
See [follow output selection](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/follow#output-selection-and-export).

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/export-filters

# Export filters

Export filters operate on **saved records**, without contacting the API. They
do not change backup contents, pagination or which objects the server returns.
Use request parameters for server-side filtering and these options for an
exported subset.

`export --where` accepts one comparison:

```text
FIELD OP VALUE
```

| Part | Accepted syntax |
|------|-----------------|
| `FIELD` | A record field or nested path such as `metadata.score`; no spaces or parentheses |
| `OP` | `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` |
| `VALUE` | Integer, decimal, or text; optional matching single/double quotes |

Quote the whole expression for your shell:

```bash
apibackuper export selected.jsonl --where "id >= 3"
apibackuper export selected.jsonl --where "metadata.score < 50"
apibackuper export selected.jsonl --where "title == 'Item 3'"
apibackuper export recent.jsonl --where "updated_at >= 2026-01-03"
```

Text containing comparison symbols, quotes of the other kind, parentheses or
the words AND/OR/NOT needs matching quotes around the value, for example
`--where "title == 'Research AND Development'"`. Embedded quotes matching the
value delimiter and backslash escape sequences are not supported by the filter
parser. Use the other delimiter or transform the exported data downstream.

## Values and comparisons

- Values parse as integers, then as decimals when they contain `.`. Matching
  quotes are stripped before this conversion, so `'123'` also becomes a number.
- Other values are strings. `true`, `false` and `null` are strings, not JSON
  boolean/null literals. There is no boolean or null literal syntax.
- A missing field or JSON `null` never matches, including `!=` conditions.
- Equality uses the decoded JSON/Python value types; numeric `3` differs from
  string `"3"`. Ordering between incompatible types does not match.
- Dates/timestamps compare as **strings**, without date parsing or timezone
  conversion. Lexicographic order is chronological only with a consistently
  normalized representation. Normalize offsets, precision and date format first.
- Nested field lookup uses `settings.splitter`, default `.`.

There are no logical expressions (`AND`, `OR`, `NOT`), chained comparisons,
parentheses, SQL `=`, `IN`, wildcard matching or regular expressions. Invalid
expressions exit with status 1 before replacing existing export output. An empty
filter string means no filter. To combine conditions, filter downstream or use
an API-side query in [params.json](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/http-requests).

## Selecting fields

```bash
apibackuper export selected.jsonl --fields id,metadata.score --where "id >= 3"
```

Filtering runs before projection. Selected nested paths become literal output
keys: `metadata.score` produces `{"metadata.score": 30}`, not a nested object.
Missing and null-valued selected fields are omitted; `0`, `false` and empty
strings are preserved. Selecting no fields leaves the original record intact.

Neither option deduplicates update history. See [export](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/export) for
source selection, retained generations and output safety.


## Worked input and output

Assume the extracted records are:

```json
[
  {"id":41,"title":"First","metadata":{"score":10}},
  {"id":42,"title":"Second","metadata":{"score":30}},
  {"id":43,"title":"Third"}
]
```

Run:

```bash
apibackuper export selected.jsonl --where "id >= 42" --fields id,title,metadata.score
```

The JSON Lines output is:

```jsonl
{"id":42,"title":"Second","metadata.score":30}
{"id":43,"title":"Third"}
```

Both IDs satisfy the condition. ID 43 remains present even though the selected
score field is missing; the missing output key is simply omitted. The filter
can read fields that are not included in `--fields` because filtering happens
before projection.

## Missing values and numeric-looking strings

| Record field | Condition | Result |
|--------------|-----------|--------|
| `score: 0` | `score == 0` | Match |
| `score: null` or missing | `score != 0` | No match |
| `id: "42"` (JSON string) | `id == 42` | No match |
| `id: "42"` | `id == '42'` | No match; quoting does not disable numeric conversion |
| `updated_at: "2026-01-03"` | `updated_at >= 2026-01-02` | String comparison matches this normalized date format |

The table uses shorthand for record values, not separate configuration fields.
Boolean record values follow Python comparison rules and may compare equal to
numeric 0/1; there is no distinct typed-boolean filter literal. For identifiers
stored as numeric-looking strings, explicit date parsing, null predicates or
compound conditions, perform the transformation/filter downstream.

## Shell quoting and invalid expressions

The shell must pass the expression as one argument. For a text value with
spaces, use outer double quotes and inner single quotes:

```bash
apibackuper export selected.jsonl --where "title == 'Item 42'"
```

`id = 42`, `id >` and `id > 1 AND id < 50` are invalid filters. They fail with
status 1 rather than creating an unfiltered or misleading export. Existing
output is preserved on failure. In Python, pass `where="id >= 42"` and a list
such as `fields=["id", "title"]`; the shell quoting layer is not needed.

Field paths use object keys and the configured splitter, not JSONPath, array
index expressions or SQL. Projecting `metadata.score` deliberately produces a
flat output key of that name. Need nested output objects or a latest-version
view of update history? Export the required fields and transform them downstream.

## Quick checks

| Unexpected result | Likely explanation |
|-------------------|--------------------|
| No rows match a visible ID | Source ID is a string, while filter value was converted to a number |
| Nulls remain absent with `!=` | Missing/null fields never match a condition |
| Date boundary seems wrong | Mixed timezone offsets, precision or non-normalized string formats |
| A nested field disappears | It was missing/null in that record, or the configured splitter differs |
| Repeated IDs remain | Filtering/projection do not deduplicate retained generations |
| Records differ from list backup | An existing unnamed follow details archive is selected for export |

---

Source: https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/getting-started/troubleshooting

# Troubleshooting

Start with the failing command and its latest exit status. Preserve saved
archives, checkpoints and recovery sidecars while investigating. `info` describes
saved successful state and can still show an earlier success after a later run
fails; a file on disk is not enough to establish that the latest collection
completed.

## Locate the failing stage

| Stage | First check | Network? |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| Installation/command startup | `python -m apibackuper --help` | No API request |
| Configuration | `apibackuper validate-config --strict` | Offline |
| Execution plan | `apibackuper run full --dry-run` | Offline |
| Endpoint/permissions/response | `apibackuper estimate full` with valid total metadata | Live sample |
| Page collection | Latest `run`/`update` exit status and log | Live requests |
| Export | Saved source, extraction key, filter and output path | Offline |
| Details/files | Source stage finished and matching configuration present | Live follow/download requests |

The default log is `apibackuper.log` in the **process working directory**.
`settings.logfile` can select another path. `--verbose` adds console logging on
`create`, `detect`, `run`, `update`, `export` and `validate-config`; it is not a
universal flag. Use `<command> --help` for its supported options.

Record the exact command, working directory, package version (`python -m pip show
apibackuper`), config format and first relevant error before changing settings.
Change one cause at a time and validate again.

## Command or module not found

If `apibackuper` is missing but this works:

```bash
python -m apibackuper --help
```

reactivate the environment that installed it or use module invocation. If the
module is also missing, run `python -m pip show apibackuper` with that interpreter
and install into the intended environment. A dependency installed in another
Python/tool-manager environment is not available to this CLI. See
[installation](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/getting-started/installation).

## Configuration not found or edits have no effect

Select the project explicitly from its parent directory:

```bash
apibackuper validate-config --strict -p catalog
apibackuper run full --dry-run -p catalog
```

Check the directory and exact filenames. The loader tries `apibackuper.yaml`,
then `apibackuper.yml`, then legacy `apibackuper.cfg`; it does not merge them.
An old YAML file can mask edits to INI. `create` supplies a minimal INI scaffold,
so a new project still needs an actual API definition.

YAML indentation, unknown keys and wrong value types fail validation. Fix the
reported path rather than moving options arbitrarily between sections. An INI
deprecation warning also makes `--strict` fail; migrate to a complete YAML
configuration rather than hiding the warning.

## Unresolved environment variable or rejected credential

`${API_TOKEN}` must be non-empty in the environment launching the process.
A `.env` file is not loaded automatically. Expansion applies to YAML strings,
not request JSON files.

For file-backed credentials, check the absolute path, readable/non-empty content
and whether an inline value overrides the file. The file contains just the
credential, without a `Bearer ` prefix or JSON wrapper. Changes to the file do
not update a running process; launch a new command with the current credential.

HTTP 401 usually requires checking credential value/expiry and any supported
refresh contract. HTTP 403 requires checking permissions, scope and endpoint
policy; OAuth refresh is triggered by 401, not 403. A successful dry-run has not
tested access. See [authentication](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/auth) and
[protected APIs](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/use-cases/protected-apis).

## Connection refused, timeout or TLS failure

For the local walkthrough, check that the server terminal is still running and
its port matches `project.url`. `127.0.0.1` refers to the machine/process network
environment running the CLI; a server on another host/container needs appropriate
routing rather than the same loopback URL.

For a real API, inspect the endpoint, network/proxy environment and error before
changing timeouts. The active fields are:

```yaml
request:
  connect_timeout: 10
  read_timeout: 120
  verify_ssl: true
```

The legacy `request.timeout` does not replace the connection/read pair. Read
timeout bounds waits for data, not total collection duration. A longer timeout
does not solve a wrong URL, rejected credentials or an unavailable service.

Keep SSL verification enabled while correcting endpoint/trust/proxy problems.
For an explicitly trusted internal/test endpoint where verification is deliberately
disabled, `request.verify_ssl: false` is supported and logs a warning. The option
is boolean, not a CA-bundle path. See
[SSL and proxies](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/rate-limiting-and-requests#ssl-and-redirects).

## HTTP 429 or repeated transient errors

Fit the request policy to the service quota, for example:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  enabled: true
  requests_per_second: 2
  requests_per_minute: 100
  burst_size: 1
request:
  parallelism: 1
  retry:
    max_retries: 3
    backoff_strategy: exponential
    initial_delay: 1
    max_delay: 10
    retry_on_status: [429, 500, 502, 503, 504]
```

Use provider-approved values. Account for other processes/apps using the same
quota; the project's limiter is per process. A Retry-After value can cause
waits longer than `max_delay`. Minute/hour windows and retries can also explain
long pauses without new requests. More concurrency or retries can worsen quota
failures. See [request policy](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/rate-limiting-and-requests).

## Only the first page, repeated pages or no apparent end

Inspect a successful response and two successive requests:

| Observation | Check |
|-------------|-------|
| First page only | Correct parameter for the chosen `iterate_by`; configured page size matches the actual server cap |
| Same IDs on every page | Page/offset field accepted by the API, including nested POST body path |
| Too many pages | Record total versus page count, stale/incorrect count, server ignoring pagination |
| A full-size page ends collection unexpectedly | Configured/fallback page boundary and usable count metadata |
| Configured `data_key` missing | Changed wrapper or an error/login response inside HTTP 200 |

`total_number_key` means records and `pages_number_key` means pages. Setting
one to the other can produce an incorrect boundary. A page shorter than
`page_size_limit` ends collection, so a requested size of 100 with an actual
cap of 50 can stop early. Skip mode computes offsets; native zero-based pages
are not supported. Cursors and next links need `iterate_by: cursor`, `next_url`
or `link_header`.

`detect` can suggest selected keys but cannot prove the contract. See
[pagination](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/pagination) and
[backup completeness](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/getting-started/data-integrity).

## Estimate fails even though collection is possible

The live estimate requires a usable `data.total_number_key`, a positive page
size and a matching record extraction path. It does not use update filters just
because its mode argument says `update`. APIs with only page-count metadata or
short-page termination can still be backed up after manual contract verification.
Use dry-run for the offline plan and do not invent a record total to satisfy
estimate. See [estimate](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/estimate).

## Resume does not continue

| Message/symptom | Action |
|-----------------|--------|
| `No valid checkpoint is available to resume` | Check selected project, checkpoint location/readability and its JSON contents |
| Checkpoint mode mismatch | Use the original full/update mode |
| Checkpoint belongs to another storage path | Recover at the matching location; do not rewrite a path casually |
| Checkpoint storage missing | Restore the referenced archive/staging and its sidecar together |
| `Backup is already complete` | This checkpoint is done; a new collection uses a fresh command without `--resume` |

Use `run full --resume` for a staged full backup and `update --resume` for its
update generation. `run continue` scans published flat page names and does not
recover full staging. Follow recovery instead uses `follow continue`.

Custom relative state/checkpoint paths resolve from the working directory, even
with `-p`. Lifecycle checkpoints are written when the periodic interval is 0.
Keep `.partial` storage and any matching `.journal` sidecar; the journal may hold
saved pages. If downloading finished before interruption, resume may complete
publication and state recovery without more HTTP requests. See [run](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/commands/run).

## Pages were saved but the command failed

Missing pages, exhausted requests, extraction failures or unsuccessful storage/
publication keep a run incomplete. `continue_on_error: true` permits later
requests but does not turn gaps into success. The checkpoint advances only
through contiguous saved progress; recover from the first unresolved page with
the matching command.

Successful state/watermark remains unchanged. A previous published full archive
can still be exported, while an incomplete update can already have pages in main
storage. Recover updates before using their export as a verified dataset. Do not
edit state/checkpoint counters to bypass the failure.

## Empty, unexpected or repeated export records

First inspect `info`, then the saved source and extraction paths. Do not replace
an existing backup with a fresh full run merely to diagnose an empty export.

- An existing unnamed `details.zip` with follow configured becomes the export
  source; its `follow_data_key` differs from the main `data_key`.
- A missing/null field never matches a `--where` condition. Numeric-looking
  filter values are converted to numbers, so a string ID may not match.
- `--fields` omits missing/null selected fields; nested paths become literal
  flat output keys.
- Original pages and retained update generations all contribute records;
  `item_key` does not deduplicate repeated IDs.
- `.json` selects JSON Lines, so a whole-file JSON-array parser is inappropriate.

Try an unfiltered export to a **new** filename, then compare representative
records. See [filter grammar](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/configuration/export-filters) and
[export verification](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/use-cases/export-and-storage).

## Parquet, output path or disk-space failure

Install optional dependencies into the environment running the command:

```bash
python -m pip install 'apibackuper[recommended]'
```

Fields with conflicting types are exported as JSON text columns. If Parquet still
fails, check for records that are not objects; JSONL keeps them as they are.
Create the output parent directory and keep the filename outside source storage.
Filesystem backups reject export anywhere under their own root. Export replaces
existing output only after success, but it needs space for the temporary output.
Full backup publication can also need old and staged storage at the same time.

## Follow or attachment collection is incomplete

| Symptom | Check |
|---------|-------|
| Missing follow ID | Separate `follow_item_key` configured and present on every list record |
| Old detail objects skipped | `follow continue` reuses names; use a deliberate full refresh for existing IDs |
| Missing unnamed details | Named rule archives are not automatic sources for normal export/getfiles |
| Unsupported file source | `getfiles` requires ZIP main storage |
| New attachment links ignored | `allfiles.csv` discovery cache must be refreshed after source updates |
| A different/updated file is skipped | Destination-name collision or existing filename; no content revalidation |
| aria2 command finished but files are absent | Running RPC service, queued transfer status and separate output/policy |

See [follow and files](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/use-cases/follow-and-files) before clearing caches or
moving outputs. Preserve the source collection while investigating.

## Prepare a useful diagnostic report

Include the exact command and working directory, Python/package versions,
selected config format, sanitized relevant sections, a small sanitized response
showing the wrapper/pagination and the first causal error. Note whether the
failure was a first full run, recovery, update, follow or export.

Review logs and samples for secrets and private data before sharing. Report
saved-state status separately from the latest command result, and retain the
original recovery files locally. See [community](https://ruarxive.org/apibackuper/development/community) for
project support channels.
